title: eMudhra intermediate CA compromise
author: galadran
relevanceReason: 命中 3 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores.

To demonstrate that the keys are compromised, the original reporter Wayne signed the following message with the private key of each of the eight intermediate CAs and reported it to the Root Program Teams on the 17th of October:
We have a problem here - Wayne
summaryZh: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores.

Since I haven't seen this mentioned enough yet:

The private key for all 8 "compromised" CAs is a single byte: https://mastodon.catgirl.cloud/@49016/117474217042191790

One of the private keys is literally "4".

I'm putting "compromised" in quotes here, because I can't call it that without cringing and cursing.

[cf. also: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50169109]

children.author: neya
children.textRawHtml: These clowns were responsible for getting a key as part of the process of getting an import/export license in India. It used to be a requirement to get a USB hardware key from them. India doesn't have any stringent data protection laws, so nothing will happen to them, even. None of their customers will actually even get to know about this incident unless they hear about it from elsewhere as most of the times, Indian companies never communicate such breaches to their customers (Eg. Domino's Pizza India had a massive breach and they never even sent as much as an email). It's really a sad state for privacy.

children.author: e28eta
children.textRawHtml:
Someone answering “questions for emudhra” also say the keys were intended to be exported to US and EU data centers. I don’t know if that would have precluded inspection (hopefully it’s encrypted some way, but why not have the destination HSM generate the CSR?)

Edit: I see the below paragraph is quoted extensively below. I hadn’t seen those comments yet. Oh well

Source: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2083449#c11

Content:

We have done some preliminary assessment, there appears to be a flaw in the KGC script that was used on that specific day to create these ECC issuers. As for these ECC keys, our review of the KGC, assessment of the code and view of HSM keys so far indicate that a) a set of original ECC keys were created onboard as expected b) an approved deviation to our usual KGC to test a wrap/unwrap was introduced as these keys were meant for export for this instance c) a flaw in the code resulted in the second pair of keys being created onboard which were weaker d) these second pair of weaker keys were used by mistake to create the csr (because the key labels were similar) and signed by our root e) the CSR from these weaker keys were also sent over to Sectigo for cross signing (we verified the files sent over to Sectigo)

The RSA issuers went through a different path as per our assessment of the code and are therefore not impacted. Some additional context - these issuers created were meant for export to our US and European data centers to solve data sovereignty issues for some of our customers (but never ended up operationally in production except for one).

children.author: mjg59
children.textRawHtml: Wrapping/unwrapping means the HSM would generate the private key and then encrypt it with a key only known to the other HSMs. Those other HSMs would then decrypt the key on import. The private key should still have been impossible to examine outside the HSMs.
